newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels vow to keep guns.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels vow to keep guns.

text.p: Albanian rebels with tanks and anti-aircraft guns vowed on Friday to fight government troops and rejected an amnesty offer by President Sali Berisha.
"Berisha is in no position to offer anything. The choice is clear. He either resigns or we all die," said Agron, a local rebel leader.
He stood by one of two Soviet-made tanks blocking Sarande's entrance while a dozen comrades, armed with Kalashnikov rifles, searched cars and people entering or leaving the town.
Berisha, facing a six-day uprising in Sarande, set a 48-hour deadline from Friday during which the rebels could return their weapons seized from army barracks in return for amnesty.

But a local rebel council, now in control, told a mass rally weapons would be returned only if Berisha resigned and immediate elections were held. Another rebel stronghold, Vlore, has already rejected the government offer and the town of Tepelene, to the north, was expected to follow suit.

"We are not giving up the weapons until Berisha resigns. Down with the dictatorship," Fuat Karali, a member of the council, told a boisterus crowd of 3,000 in Sarande's main square. "Don't be afraid. He has no army."

State buildings were burned during the uprising, thousands of weapons were seized from nearby barracks and former military officers joined forces with the rebels to defend against a possible crackdown by forces loyal to Berisha.

The officers organised the rebels into units who dug in on hilltops, safely hid heavy artillery and put in force a night curfew. Anti-aircraft machineguns were placed in key positions and camouflage was used to cover them.

"People of Sarande. This town must be defended and become organised. There will be no more shooting for no reason. Parents will take weapons away from kids under 18. The shops must open and there is nothing to fear," said Javar, a former army colonel. "Those breaking the rules will be arrested."
Sarande sits in the far southwestern corner of the small Balkan country, just across from the Greek island of Corfu and just north of the Greek border.
For six days locals have run riot, firing rifles in the air, driving a seized tank around town and sporting headscarves and ghoulish masks to hide their faces.
Three people have been sent to Corfu with bullet wounds and the town hospital was running short of blood, plasma, gauze and stitches.

"We are on alert because we will have many injuries if the army comes down. People were also shot by accident. We urgently need a portable X-ray machine to locate the bullets," Petraq Kaci, the hospital director, told Reuters.
In one of the rooms, two beaten up secret police members, accused of being sent to collect information from Tirana, were handcaffed on their beds awaiting a "people's court" verdict on them.
"Berisha sent me here. I regret what I did. I apologise ... I am with the people," said one of them, Eduart Aliaz.
Rebel groups clashed in nearby hills with about 60 army regulars on Wednesday but has been mostly quiet since.
Army units -- four tanks and some soldiers -- were seen on Thursday some 60 km (36 miles) away on the main north-south road at the Muzine junction which leads to Sarande.

"We have shortages for the first time in bread, flour and gas. What we get we get from Corfu when boat owners are not afraid to travel," said Thoma Mico, a parliament deputy, representing the Greek minority in southern Albania.
